
Advanced nodes change the values, but they do not remove the cost of moving
data or driving wires. The comparison remains a useful reminder that locality
belongs in the architecture model before candidates are ranked.

A useful architecture-level decomposition is
$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} =
E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} +
E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} +
E_{\mathrm{leakage}} .
$$
This is a decomposition, not a circuit-level energy model, and it carries a diminishing-returns lesson. Optimizing the compute term yields shrinking system-level returns once the unoptimized data-movement and leakage terms dominate the power budget. It helps an architect
check whether the comparison includes every major source of energy that could
change the decision. A candidate that reduces arithmetic but increases memory
movement, interconnect traffic, control overhead, or leakage may make the
system worse. Nothing requires memory energy to rise when compute energy falls,
but an optimization focused on one term can allow the others to grow enough to
exceed the baseline total (@fig-waterbed-effect). For example, an automated search might aggressively optimize a Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) array's arithmetic energy. However, to keep thousands of MACs fed, the Network-on-Chip (NoC) may have to route data across the die, incurring heavy wire-toggling costs. An early proxy might rank the compute-heavy design first, but the candidate ultimately fails because it creates unroutable congestion.

![**Lower compute energy can hide a worse system total.** The illustrative candidate reduces compute energy but increases memory and interconnect energy enough to exceed the baseline total. A comparison that omits data movement can therefore rank the worse of the two designs first. The bar heights show the relationship and are not measured energy breakdowns.](images/F2-waterbed-effect){#fig-waterbed-effect width="85%" fig-alt="Bar chart comparing a baseline energy breakdown with an illustrative candidate whose lower compute energy is outweighed by higher memory and interconnect energy."}

The baseline and candidate in the figure differ in more than arithmetic. The
candidate lowers the compute term, but its added memory traffic and
communication raise the system total above the baseline. The numbers are
illustrative, but the reversal is the point. An early proxy can favor a design
that loses once the comparison includes the costs of moving data through the system. This is the proxy-mismatch failure that @sec-feedback-verification-trust treats directly.

Interconnect costs deserve the same attention as memory movement. On-chip
networks, package links, memory interfaces, collectives, and host-device
protocols limit what a design can sustain. Early logical synthesis and
architecture models use approximate interconnect estimates, while placement and
routing expose the actual topology, congestion, and parasitic delays. A highly
parallel accelerator can therefore score well in an early model and fail timing
or routing after physical implementation. The failure is not that early tools
ignore wires entirely. It is that an optimizer can exploit whatever the
inexpensive model leaves out.

Timing, placement, routing, IR drop, thermal behavior, power delivery, leakage, signoff, and test may also overturn an architectural choice, so architects must consider the relevant EDA and physical-design constraints early. These checks rely on stateful tools, and a repeated run can be invalid if stale constraints or cached netlists survive from an earlier candidate. @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces treats the tool isolation and execution mechanics. Here the point is that a clean tool state is part of a valid comparison. Power and thermal density can flag a dense accelerator mapping as risky before implementation. For the Lighthouse, the 3\ W limit is not only a battery constraint but a skin-temperature constraint on a face-worn device, and a dense MAC array can pass an average-TDP check while creating a localized hotspot that makes the headset unwearable.

Later IR-drop and thermal signoff can confirm or clear that risk once a placed
netlist and current profile exist. Thermal design power (TDP), a target for
sizing the cooling solution rather than a measure of sustained draw, is not the
only limit. A large specialized vector unit can create a rapid current change
when many lanes become active, producing voltage droop that constrains safe
operation. Early physical estimates, workload-aware power models, and closer
coordination between microarchitecture and physical design can expose that risk
before final signoff.

::: {.callout-field-note title="A behavior to measure in AVX-512 studies"}
**The expectation.** Adding 512-bit vector units to general-purpose CPU cores
raises peak floating-point throughput.

**Example to verify.** Sustained wide-vector execution raises instantaneous
power and power-delivery demand, and some processors may reduce frequency under
these conditions. The policy and magnitude are implementation-specific.

**The lesson.** Peak vector width does not determine application speed by
itself. The architect must measure the active-frequency policy and the mix of
vector and nonvector work on the processor being evaluated.
:::

Signoff runs these checks across multiple process, voltage, temperature, and
operating-mode combinations. A design may clear one Multi-Corner Multi-Mode
(MCMM) scenario and fail another, and which corner is critical depends on the
process, cell library, voltage, and path. Because physical-design tools use
heuristic optimization, one failed closure attempt may not reveal whether the
candidate or the tool setup caused the failure. Comparing constraints, seeds,
and repeated outcomes helps separate the two.

Design Rule Checks (DRC) add another physical constraint. Advanced-node rule
decks contain many geometrical requirements, including coloring, via enclosure,
and metal spacing. Moving one macro can create many violations, and repairing
one can change neighboring routes and expose others. An automated flow that
cannot interpret those markers leaves repeated cleanup and rerouting work for
the implementation team.

Automation adds a traceability problem to each of these physical constraints. If
a generator emits high-level RTL and a physical-design tool reports a thermal
failure later, tracing that result to the design decision that caused it can be
difficult. A saved RTL or topology artifact can be rerun even when generation
was stochastic, which is why the project must preserve the emitted artifact,
parameters, tool state, and lineage rather than depend on regeneration.
Evaluating physical constraints also requires bridging the semantic gap between
high-level proposals and EDA formats such as LEF/DEF and Liberty timing
files.[^fn-lef-def-c02]

[^fn-lef-def-c02]: **LEF/DEF and Liberty**: The interchange formats a physical-design flow actually runs on, where LEF describes a standard cell's abstract geometry and pin locations, DEF records the placed and routed instance of one specific design, and a Liberty file holds a cell library's characterized timing and power at one corner. They are verbose and positional rather than semantic, so a generator fluent in RTL is far less able to emit or read them than the source it was trained on.

The predictive models that screen microarchitectural configurations have a
general form. Multifidelity methods combine many inexpensive estimates with
selected high-fidelity evaluations and retain the stronger model to check
accuracy, a strategy that runs across engineering optimization rather than
architecture alone [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. Physical constraints
require the same care. If an early model omits timing, congestion, thermal
behavior, or data movement, the architect needs a better model before generating
more candidates.

For the 3\ nm-class mobile XR subsystem comparison, a cheap energy proxy can support early
screening, but finalists need a current power model before they can support a
power or efficiency decision.

Choosing the wrong term to optimize is not only an energy-model failure. A
design can lead on the figures a data sheet reports and still fall behind on the
work a real program does.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** AMD's Bulldozer [@Cutress2014FX9590] generation (Zambezi, 2011) bet that many simpler integer cores sharing a front-end and a floating-point unit, pushed to high clock speeds, would win on the numbers buyers and reviewers compared most directly, core count and clock frequency.

**The gap.** Those figures ignored how a real workload used the machine. The shared front-end and floating-point unit starved per-thread execution, so single-thread performance trailed even AMD's own previous generation, and raising clocks to compensate drove power up (the later FX-9590 part carried a 220\ W rating [@Cutress2014FX9590]).

**The lesson.** Rank a candidate on the metric its workload rewards, not the number that is easiest to count. In silicon that gap is expensive to discover, because it appears only after the design has shipped. Restoring competitive per-thread performance took a clean-sheet microarchitecture, Zen [@AMDZen], several years later.
:::

These physical constraints and reliability concerns define an enormous search
space, and machine learning models can predict performance and power usefully
from early design stages [@LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling]. A learned dynamic
IR-drop estimator, for example, can screen candidates much faster than a
commercial analysis tool [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet]. Novel topologies may fall
outside the data that support such a model. Uncertainty estimates or
distribution-shift checks can warn about some cases, but selected candidates
still need the stronger physical tools required by the claim. The method
comparison in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization decides when that
screening role repays its data, compute, and evaluation cost.

### The Evaluation Budget {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

Architects cannot run every candidate through every available tool.
Simulation, synthesis, physical design, emulation, verification, and expert
review consume different mixtures of compute, licenses, schedule, and human
attention. Feedback becomes scarce when the project requires more of that work
than the available people and tools can provide.

Evaluation tools form a spectrum whose tiers can sit orders of magnitude apart
in throughput, cost, and setup time. As an illustrative calculation rather than
a universal rate, a simulator running at ten to one hundred thousand
instructions per second needs roughly three to twenty-eight hours to represent
one second of a workload retiring one billion instructions per second.
Emulation and FPGA prototypes can run faster, but require different hardware,
compilation, and bring-up costs. Actual rates depend on the model, workload,
host, tool, and platform. The budget question is therefore not only whether a
candidate can be measured, but which candidates earn an expensive tier.

Active-learning and surrogate-guided methods can direct expensive EDA runs
toward candidates that appear most informative, and such methods have
accelerated architectural exploration in practice
[@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. They still consume training data and evaluation
budget. Statistical sampling addresses the same pressure in another way, with
SimPoint selecting representative program regions
[@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint] and SMARTS bounding the error of sampled simulation
[@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Whether any of these approaches repays its cost is
a method-selection question for
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. The point here is narrower.
Expensive evaluation can limit how many candidates receive a decisive check.

The allocation decision is itself difficult. Generating or scoring another
candidate may be cheap, but an inaccurate screen can discard a useful design or
send a weak one into an expensive stage. The architect must decide which
inexpensive checks can reject a candidate safely, which uncertainties require
stronger tools, and which measurements are likely to change the decision.
Otherwise, faster generation adds more work to the project's most
expensive stages.

Leading-edge chip-development costs show the scale of this constraint. Public
estimates vary and should not be treated as universal accounting rules. The
Semiconductor Industry Association reports that the cost of designing a
latest-node chip rose from about \$30M for a 65\ nm chip in 2006 to more than
\$540M for a 5\ nm chip in 2020, a greater than $18\times$ increase
[@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign]. A McKinsey analysis
gives a similar order of magnitude, estimating roughly \$175M for a 10\ nm
design, \$300M for a 7\ nm design, and \$540M for a 5\ nm design when validation,
IP qualification, and related development costs are included
[@BauerEtAl2020SemiconductorDesignManufacturing]. These estimates include more
than masks or wafers. They reflect architecture, design, validation,
verification, IP, tools, and engineering labor.

The most expensive tier carries a sticker price of its own. A full mask set at
a leading node can run to tens of millions of dollars, an order-of-magnitude
anchor rather than a quoted price. A respin may replace a subset or a larger
share of those masks and adds fabrication, validation, and schedule cost before
the team learns whether the correction worked. Simulation, emulation, and
signoff exist in part to reduce the chance of paying for that iteration again.

### The Verification Bottleneck

Verification faces an exponential state-space upper bound, although structure,
abstraction, and verification methods determine the work a project actually
performs. Adding one state-holding bit doubles the number of encoded states, so
a design with $n$ such bits can encode as many as $2^n$ states. The reachable
subset is usually far smaller and depends on reset and next-state logic, which
is why verification does not amount to enumerating every encoded state.

No project verifies a design in the exhaustive sense; the $2^n$ arithmetic forecloses that on the first page. Teams instead combine coverage goals, assertions, formal results, constrained-random testing, regressions, unresolved-defect review, and engineering judgment. A flattening bug-discovery curve is one input to the tapeout decision, not the decision rule by itself. A flood of novel candidates asks the team to repeat substantial parts of that work.

Architectural evaluation must therefore consider verification work alongside
Power, Performance, and Area (PPA). A speculative cache-coherence protocol
might offer a measured performance gain yet still be a poor choice if its
additional states and interactions cannot be checked within the project budget.

Formal verification and simulation both face limits as sequential state and
component interactions grow. Whether verification limits a particular project
remains a measurement question rather than a given. Every novel architectural
variant still creates verification work. Generating testbench collateral may
reduce part of that work [@QiuEtAl2024AutoBench], but the resulting design and
collateral still require independent checks. Sequential model checking,
including Bounded Model Checking (BMC), also faces state growth. Combinational
equivalence checking avoids sequential state by checking a different property,
while sequential behavior continues to require a mix of formal and simulation
methods [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

The industry has described verification pressure for a quarter century. The
2001 ITRS Design chapter called verification "a bottleneck that has now reached
crisis proportions" [@ITRS2001Design], and the Semiconductor Research
Corporation's MAPT roadmap still lists a widening verification gap among the
transitions ahead [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. This history
makes verification a condition worth checking in any proposal to generate
architectural candidates faster. It does not establish that verification is
the limiting condition in every project.

If a search outputs dozens of novel RTL accelerators a week, but a verification engineer requires weeks to write the testbenches and covergroups for just one, the generation speed is wasted. This gap grounds the state-space explosion in the daily reality of an RTL team. Foster's summary of the 2022 Wilson Research Group functional-verification study reports that demand for IC/ASIC verification engineers grew nearly three times as much as demand for design engineers from 2007 to 2022, about 146 percent versus 50 percent (@fig-verification-demand-scissors). Mean peak staffing was roughly one verification engineer per design engineer across most market segments, processor projects reached ratios as high as five to one, and design engineers spent 49 percent of their time on verification in 2022 [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Every invalid candidate that reaches these stages consumes compute and scarce engineering time. Generated candidates are cheap only until they require tools, verification, and expert review.

That staffing ratio suggests a hypothesis rather than a project diagnosis. If
verification packages are waiting for engineers, a generator that drafts
covergroups and testbenches may reduce part of that work, while a generator that
adds novel blocks may enlarge the queue. If packages are not waiting there, the
same intervention addresses the wrong problem. Only local observations can
distinguish those cases.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Verification staffing grew faster than design staffing.** Mean peak demand for IC/ASIC verification engineers grew about 146 percent from 2007 to 2022 while demand for design engineers grew about 50 percent, a 6.2 versus 2.7 percent compound annual growth rate [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Filled markers have printed data labels in the published study figures; hollow 2022 markers are chart-read approximations constrained by the study's stated growth figures.
#| out-width: "78%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-line chart indexing engineer demand to 2007, with verification-engineer demand rising to about 2.5 times its 2007 level by 2022 while design-engineer demand reaches about 1.5 times, opening a widening gap between the lines."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Mean peak engineers per IC/ASIC project, Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA
# functional-verification studies (Foster's published summaries). 2007-2020
# values have printed data labels; 2022 values are chart-read, constrained by
# the study's stated callouts of +50% design and +146% verification demand
# growth since 2007 (2.7% vs 6.2% CAGR).
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv
years = [2007, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2022]
design = [7.8, 8.5, 10.5, 10.3, 11.7]
verif = [4.8, 8.4, 11.6, 11.4, 11.8]

design_idx = [v / design[0] for v in design]
verif_idx = [v / verif[0] for v in verif]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.80, top=0.93, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(years, verif_idx, color=COLORS["green"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.plot(years, design_idx, color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(years[:-1], verif_idx[:-1], s=22, color=COLORS["green"], zorder=3)
ax.scatter(years[:-1], design_idx[:-1], s=20, marker="s", color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
# 2022 values are chart-read approximations: draw them hollow
ax.scatter([years[-1]], [verif_idx[-1]], s=26, facecolors="white",
           edgecolors=COLORS["green"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([years[-1]], [design_idx[-1]], s=24, marker="s", facecolors="white",
           edgecolors=COLORS["blue"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)

ax.text(2022.6, verif_idx[-1], "verification\nengineers (+146%)", va="center",
        fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["green"], clip_on=False)
ax.text(2022.6, design_idx[-1], "design\nengineers (+50%)", va="center",
        fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["blue"], clip_on=False)

ax.set_xlim(2006, 2023)
ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.7)
ax.set_xticks([2007, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2022])
ax.set_yticks([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1.0$\\times$", "1.5$\\times$", "2.0$\\times$", "2.5$\\times$"])
ax.set_ylabel("mean peak demand vs. 2007", fontsize=7)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The two lines in @fig-verification-demand-scissors are indexed to their 2007
values, so they show relative growth rather than absolute staffing levels. The
verification line rises much faster. The staffing data do not establish a
single cause for that difference, and they do not identify the cause of any one
project's difficulty. They do show that checking designs has consumed a growing
share of engineering capacity in the surveyed projects. A generated candidate
that reaches this stage is no longer free to evaluate.

Hardware is unforgiving because a defect in shipped silicon is costly to address and never cleanly undone. The 1994 Pentium FDIV flaw shows why early checks matter, as a defect arising from five omitted lookup table entries [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision] led Intel to report a \$475M pretax charge for replacement and associated costs [@Intel1995PentiumCharge]. More recently, the Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre] exposed microarchitectural side channels in speculative execution. Software and microcode mitigations can impose workload- and processor-dependent costs without removing the underlying hardware mechanism. These episodes show how a hardware flaw becomes an expensive, long-lived liability after a design has shipped, one that replacement, support, or a software workaround can mitigate but not cleanly remove.

The Pentium charge reflects one escaped defect, but leading-edge development
raises the cost of commitment even when no public recall occurs. A 2023 report
of an IBS estimate places the cost of a large 2\ nm chip developed from scratch
without reusable IP at roughly \$725M
[@Shilov2023IBSDesignCost]. The estimate is not a
universal project price. It shows that high-fidelity evaluation and physical
implementation at the leading edge consume engineering budgets, not only
simulator cycles.

The composition of that budget matters more to an architect than its total.
Software development and verification alone account for roughly two-thirds of a
from-scratch 2\ nm design (@fig-design-cost-composition). The work that dominates
a leading-node budget is not drawing the artifact. It is writing the software
that runs on it and establishing that the design is correct.

The ranking is older than the node that produced these numbers. The 2001 ITRS
Design chapter reported that software already accounted for 80 percent of
embedded-systems development cost [@ITRS2001Design], measured on a different
accounting boundary than the figure below and so not a point on the same trend.
It is another example of substantial software cost, not evidence of a
two-decade trend between compatible measurements.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-composition
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Software and verification dominate a leading-node design budget.** International Business Strategies puts the cost of designing a large 2\ nm chip from scratch, without reusable IP, at \$725M, of which software development accounts for about \$314M and verification about \$154M [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus; @Shilov2023IBSDesignCost]. Arm's prospectus states that software, verification, and IP qualification together are 71 percent of the total, which places IP qualification near \$46M. No public source divides the remaining architecture, physical design, prototype, and validation work, so it appears here as one hatched block rather than as invented values.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "A single horizontal bar spanning $725 million, divided left to right into software development at $314 million, verification at $154 million, IP qualification at $46 million, and a hatched unallocated block of $210 million covering architecture, physical design, prototype, and validation."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Sourced constants: IBS 2 nm estimate as reported in Arm's Form 424B4
# [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus] and the IBS slide reported by Tom's Hardware
# [@Shilov2023IBSDesignCost]. IP qualification and the unallocated remainder are
# computed here from the filing's stated 71 percent share, never hand-typed.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv
total_musd = 725
software_musd = 314
verification_musd = 154
sw_ver_ip_share = 0.71

ip_qual_musd = sw_ver_ip_share * total_musd - software_musd - verification_musd
unallocated_musd = total_musd - software_musd - verification_musd - ip_qual_musd

segments = [
    ("software\ndevelopment", software_musd, COLORS["blue"], None),
    ("verification", verification_musd, COLORS["green"], None),
    ("IP\nqualification", ip_qual_musd, COLORS["orange"], None),
    ("architecture, physical design,\nprototype, validation",
     unallocated_musd, COLORS["grid"], "//"),
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 1.35))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.98, top=0.88, bottom=0.30)

left = 0.0
for label, value, colour, hatch in segments:
    ax.barh([0], [value], left=left, height=0.5, color=colour,
            edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, hatch=hatch, zorder=3)
    share = 100 * value / total_musd
    ink = COLORS["ink"] if hatch else "white"
    ax.text(left + value / 2, 0, f"{share:.0f}%", ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=6.4, color=ink, zorder=4)
    ax.text(left + value / 2, -0.36, label, ha="center", va="top",
            fontsize=5.6, color=COLORS["muted"], zorder=4)
    left += value

ax.set_xlim(0, total_musd)
ax.set_ylim(-0.95, 0.5)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks([0, 200, 400, 600, total_musd])
ax.set_xlabel("cumulative design cost for one 2 nm chip (USD millions)",
              fontsize=6.6, labelpad=2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

These estimates come from different accounting boundaries and do not form a controlled technology trend. What they do show is that the strongest evaluations and final implementation decisions take place within projects measured in hundreds of millions of dollars.

These costs change what should count as improvement. Producing more candidates
is not useful if every survivor adds simulation, synthesis, physical-design,
verification, and reviewer work to an already full queue. When results arrive faster than experts can reconcile
them, review queues grow and the project cannot close the decision. Turning scattered tool results into evidence a decision can rest on is the work of @sec-feedback-verification-trust, and @sec-running-the-loop carries one such comparison end to end under a fixed budget.

## Compounding Design Loop Pressure {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

The chapter walked the design stack by layers, from microarchitecture through
specialization, composition, software, and physics, but the diagnostic that
follows is organized by failure mode rather than by layer. A layer suggests
where to look, not what limits a project. The five candidate conditions are
missing information, unhelpful or invalid choices, expensive evaluation,
overloaded review, and an unclear decision.

The mapping is many-to-many. Microarchitecture and multicore studies may require
long runs to settle corner cases and coherence behavior. Specialization may
expose uncertainty about whether a workload will remain important or add
verification work at a new interface. System composition may hide information
inside third-party blocks, while warehouse-scale studies may lack a reproducible
production traffic mix. A software description can become stale, and physical
checks can consume expensive tool and reviewer time. An unclear decision has no
home layer because it can follow any of them. These are reasons to inspect the
work, not evidence that one condition limits a particular project.

Each problem described above can stall architecture work on its own. In
practice, they reinforce one another. Specialization expands the choice set,
each hardware choice creates software obligations, software changes can make
the workload description stale, and physical effects can reverse the remaining
rankings. The strongest checks then arrive at the point where tools and
engineering attention are most expensive.

AI may solve one problem and create another elsewhere. Faster
generation can fill an evaluation queue. Faster simulation can produce more
results than reviewers can settle. A better physical model can reveal that the
permitted choices cannot satisfy the task. The size of the design space is only
one part of the compound problem. The available information changes which
choices are legal, those choices determine what evaluation and review are
needed, and the resulting evidence determines what decision can be made.

The mobile XR subsystem example shows how the problems can accumulate. A search
may find a promising chiplet accelerator, only for the compiler path to rule out
its interface. A revised design may compile, but a newer XR trace can change its
memory behavior. A high-fidelity physical run may then expose a thermal or
data-movement cost that the early model missed. Each correction narrows the
comparison while creating new evaluation and review work. The architect has to track
those changes so that the final recommendation still answers the original
design question.

The work a project must settle and the work its tools and reviewers can examine
diverge as two lines (@fig-scissors-gap). What decides an architectural claim is
the region between them, because a candidate sitting inside it has been generated
but not evaluated well enough to accept or reject. A project can grow that region
without noticing. No tool report distinguishes a candidate that survived review
from one that never reached a reviewer.

![**Design work can outpace the capacity to examine it.** The widening region holds candidates that have been generated but never evaluated well enough to accept or reject.](images/F2-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="85%" fig-alt="Diverging-line diagram where the work created by design choices, constraints, software paths, physical questions, and evidence grows faster than tools and reviewers can examine it."}

The curves are conceptual rather than a universal time series. The search-space
examples show how quickly a project can produce candidates, while the
verification-staffing data provide one measured example of the engineering
effort needed to check increasingly complex designs. Together, they illustrate
why a mismatch between arrivals and completion capacity is plausible and worth
measuring locally.

The scissors in @fig-scissors-gap has a famous ancestor. In 1999 the
International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors measured transistor budgets
compounding at roughly 58 percent a year against designer productivity at 21
percent and named the difference the design productivity gap [@ITRS1999Roadmap]. The industry
responded to that gap in part by raising abstraction, including RTL synthesis
and IP reuse, so that one engineer's decision could govern more transistors.
Twenty-two years later the SRC and SIA restated the same shortfall
in their Decadal Plan for Semiconductors, naming a design gap between what a
technology permits and what can be designed in reasonable time and calling for a
tenfold or greater step in design productivity, though they scoped that target to
analog and mixed-signal work rather than to the loop as a whole
[@SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. That history sets the bar for what follows in this
book. AI assistance earns its place only when the project can show which work it
changes without weakening the checks needed for the decision.

A growing evaluation or review queue makes the problem visible. A project can
still be in trouble even when no queue is visible. It may be missing
information that would reverse the result, or its available choices may exclude
the design it needs.

![**Four problems can reinforce one another.** Missing information can yield invalid choices, which can waste scarce high-fidelity evaluation, overload reviewers, and leave project information less current. The figure shows one possible pattern, not a universal sequence.](images/F2-bottleneck-causal-loop){#fig-bottleneck-causal-loop width="85%" fig-alt="Four labeled nodes arranged in a possible reinforcement cycle. Missing information can lead to invalid choices, invalid choices can trigger expensive evaluation, expensive evaluation can overload review, and delayed review can leave information less current."}

The pressures can form the reinforcement pattern in
@fig-bottleneck-causal-loop. Missing information can produce choices that later
prove invalid. Those choices consume evaluation and review capacity, and delay
can make inputs less current. A project need not follow this sequence. An
unclear decision also sits outside the four-node figure and can follow any of
the other conditions. The five failure points are analytically distinct but
often coexist (@tbl-loop-bottleneck-diagnostic).

| **What goes wrong** | **Mobile XR subsystem example** | **Why more candidates do not help** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missing information | The comparison omits memory-movement cost, so a later estimate overturns the ranking of XR compute organizations. | Every new candidate is judged with the same incomplete view of the system. |
| Unhelpful or invalid choices | The allowed choices let AI retune parameters but not change the accelerator interface needed to meet both the deadline and power limit. | A larger search cannot reach a design that lies outside the permitted choices. |
| Expensive evaluation | Only a few higher-fidelity estimates are affordable, so most candidates receive only cheap estimates. | More candidates compete for the same scarce measurements. |
| Overloaded review | Proxy, simulator, and compiler results disagree across several candidates, but reviewers cannot reconcile them before the next design review. | More candidates add results to the same unresolved review queue. |
| Unclear decision | A candidate clears the available checks, but no one has stated whether that result authorizes implementation, further study, or stopping. | Additional results do not resolve what action the current evidence permits. |

: **Five problems that can keep architecture work from moving forward.** The examples show why more candidates may not help. {#tbl-loop-bottleneck-diagnostic tbl-colwidths="[24,40,36]"}

The rows separate problems that often appear together. A project with an
incomplete memory model may also lack simulation capacity and reviewer time.
Treating all three as a search limitation obscures what needs to be fixed first.
The missing model must be repaired before the architect can tell whether
evaluation or review still limits progress. If the results are complete but
waiting to be reconciled, the problem is review. If the evidence has been
reviewed but no next action is defined, the architect must decide whether it
supports more exploration, implementation, or no action at all.

Industry-wide trends can show why a diagnosis matters, but they cannot tell an
individual project what is slowing it down. Across the Wilson Research Group functional-verification studies,
first-silicon success fell from roughly one third of surveyed IC/ASIC projects
to 14 percent in 2024 [@Foster2023WilsonVerificationResults; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. The series shows unresolved risk, but it
cannot say whether the cause was design, verification, integration, physical
implementation, manufacturing, scheduling, or organization. Each project needs
its own workload, tool, review, and decision information to find the problem.

### Diagnose One Work Item

A project does not need a universal measurement system to begin. It needs one
named kind of work and a fixed observation window. The work might be a
candidate awaiting simulation, a finalist awaiting physical review, a failed
test awaiting diagnosis, or a comparison awaiting a decision. Issue trackers,
experiment records, tool queues, review history, and decision records can
usually supply a first set of observations. The fields in
@tbl-work-constraint-observations keep that first pass small.

| **Observation** | **What to record for one work item and window** | **What it helps distinguish** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work item and window | The unit entering and leaving the process, together with the start and end dates. | Whether counts and delays refer to the same work. |
| Arrivals and completions | How many items entered and how many reached the stated exit condition. | A growing queue from work that arrives faster than it completes. |
| Waiting | Where each item waited and for how long, separate from tool runtime and active engineering time. | Tool, engineering, and reviewer capacity. |
| Rework | How many items repeated a tool run, analysis, or review, and why. | Slow first-pass work from work made slow by correction and repetition. |
| Input availability and freshness | Which required inputs were present and which workload, compiler, interface, model, and tool versions each item used. | Missing or stale information from a capacity problem. |
| Choice outcome | Which candidates were rejected as illegal or unhelpful, why, and whether the allowed choices could reach the target. | An invalid or unhelpful choice set from an evaluation-capacity problem. |
| Evaluation | Tool runtime, license or compute wait, cost, fidelity, and whether the decisive check completed. | Expensive evaluation from a downstream review delay. |
| Review | When an item became ready, when review began, and why it was accepted, rejected, or returned. | Evaluation delay from overloaded or inconclusive review. |
| Decision closure | Which action the result supported, who could take it, and whether the action occurred. | Completed analysis from an unclear decision. |
| Preserved check | The measurement, tool verdict, or expert review that an intervention must leave useful. | Reduced work from a weaker architectural claim. |

: **A small observation record for diagnosing delayed architecture work.** The
fields use ordinary project records and separate how much work enters, where it
waits, why it repeats, and whether it closes a decision.
{#tbl-work-constraint-observations tbl-colwidths="[21,43,36]"}

Not every project will have every field. Missing observations leave the
diagnosis unresolved rather than proving one of the five modes. The point is to
replace a general impression that the project is slow with a supported claim
about a particular kind of work.

Consider a fifteen-working-day window for mobile XR finalist packages that need
thermal and IR-drop review. Suppose the queue begins empty, twelve packages
become ready, and three clear review, leaving nine waiting. Tool execution takes
less than one day per package, but the completed packages wait a median of eight
days for a qualified reviewer. The oldest unfinished package has waited twelve
days, which prevents the completed-only median from hiding the open work. Two of
the three completed packages also repeat analysis after a compiler update
changes the workload trace, and the architecture review is postponed because
the remaining packages have no verdict.

For this work item during this window, those observations support overloaded
review compounded by input churn. They do not show that candidate generation
or simulator throughput limits other work in the project. An intervention
should reduce the unresolved review queue, waiting time, or rework while
preserving the thermal and IR-drop verdicts. If the declared observations do
not improve under comparable conditions, the intervention failed its test and
the team should revisit the diagnosis, intervention, or observation window. A
project can have more than one limiting condition, but each one needs
observations of the work it is claimed to constrain.

## Applying AI Assistance at Bottlenecks {#sec-feedback-and-verification-become-the-bottleneck}

Once observations support one of the five diagnoses, an intervention can be
tested against the work that is delayed. The intervention might be a process
change, additional tool capacity, a clearer review rule, or AI assistance.
This chapter does not yet choose among generation, prediction, optimization, or a
conventional method. That selection belongs to
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. The examples here show only
how a possible AI role should be tied to a named problem rather than treated as
a general accelerator.

Sorted by the mode they act on rather than by the layer they came from, the chapter's own examples fall into place. Against missing information, models adapted to a company's design collateral and agents that drive tool flows from a natural-language request assemble context an engineer would otherwise gather by hand [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]. Against unhelpful or invalid choices, learned heuristics that transfer across workloads hold a large accelerator search inside the region a real compiler can target [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo]. Against expensive evaluation, surrogates trained on detailed runs rank configurations for a fraction of the cost of the tool they replace [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling], a learned estimator returns a dynamic IR-drop figure where commercial analysis takes an order of magnitude longer [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet], and uncertainty-guided triage spends the high-fidelity runs on candidates that could still change the answer [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. When local observations show that verification-authoring work is limiting, a generator that drafts testbenches may reduce part of that work [@QiuEtAl2024AutoBench]. The fifth mode is the exception, and it stays one. Organizing results for a decision is work a method can do. Deciding is not.

The same method can affect two projects differently. A surrogate may reduce
simulation work when a simulator queue delays the decision. If the workload
description is stale, the same surrogate can rank candidates against the wrong
target without reducing the actual delay. These are intervention hypotheses.
The project still has to observe whether the named queue, waiting time, rework,
or decision closure changes.

Any proposed assistance also consumes some of the project's budget. A surrogate
needs data from stronger tools, a generator can add candidates to a full queue,
and a retrieval system needs current sources. Those costs belong in the method
comparison in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. At this point,
they serve as checks against assuming that more automated activity means more
decisions.

Because the five problems in @tbl-loop-bottleneck-diagnostic differ, each admits a defined job, a named piece of engineering work that job should reduce, and a check the architect still owns (@tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound). Those three columns are what turn a claim of assistance into one a reviewer can test. A method that cannot name the problem it targets is being adopted without a supported need. One that cannot name the work it removed has no measurable benefit to report. One that cannot name the check that stayed independent of it has reduced the basis for the architectural claim along with the labor.

| **Problem** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What the architect must still establish** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Missing information | Retrieve and reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information, then flag missing variables or stale assumptions. | Manual search and synthesis across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and the architect's judgment that the available information is sufficient for the decision. |
| Unhelpful or invalid choices | Check constraints, screen illegal combinations, and identify when the permitted choices cannot satisfy the task. | Invalid tool runs and manual feasibility checks. | Tool-backed legality rules, fixed interfaces, and the architect's authority to change the design space. |
| Expensive evaluation | Screen candidates, estimate uncertainty, and select experiments for high-fidelity evaluation. | High-fidelity tool runs spent on candidates unlikely to change the decision. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design space, and the measurements that can overturn the prediction. |
| Overloaded review | Compare results under common criteria, expose disagreements, and route uncertain cases to reviewers. | Reviewer time spent sorting repeated or weak results. | Independent checks, recorded rejection reasons, and the measured capacity of the review process. |
| Unclear decision | Organize evidence and prepare it for a stated action, flagging assumptions that would reopen the decision. | Preparation and reconciliation before a design review. | The decision scope, unresolved risks, rollback conditions, and the person authorized to act. |

: **Different problems call for different AI roles.** Each row identifies the engineering work AI could reduce and what the architect must still verify or decide without relying on the model. {#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[20,29,23,28]"}

The rows are not interchangeable. A cost predictor addresses expensive
evaluation only if it reduces high-fidelity tool runs; it does not repair a
missing workload description or decide that a candidate is ready to implement.
In the mobile XR subsystem comparison, an AI ranking based on a cheap power proxy helps only
if stronger measurements test whether memory movement or physical limits
reverse that ranking. A useful evaluation of any of these methods shows whether
it reduced the targeted engineering work while preserving the evidence the
architectural claim needs.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Testing assistance against a review constraint"}
**Context.** The mobile XR subsystem comparison can stall in all five ways at
once. The observations here support overloaded review for this work item during
the named window.

**Where the work waits.** During the fifteen-working-day observation window,
twelve finalist packages become ready for thermal and IR-drop review, three
clear review, and nine remain. The completed packages spend a median of eight
days waiting for the two qualified reviewers, even though tool execution takes
less than one day. Candidates are arriving faster than they leave. Overloaded
review is the supported diagnosis, and nothing in these observations shows
that search is the constraint for this work item during this window.

**What to test.** Compare the competing proxy, simulator, and compiler results
for each finalist under common criteria and flag where they disagree before the
engineers review every finalist. This may reduce result-reconciliation work
without reducing the required physical checks or reviewer verdicts.

**What to compare.** A shared review template, different scheduling, added
review capacity, and automated result comparison could all address part of the
observed wait. A faster generator or a wider design space does not directly
address it. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization compares the
available methods after the job is defined.

**What the architect keeps.** The thermal and IR-drop verdicts stay with the
engineers and the signoff tools. The intervention prepares and prioritizes the
review. It does not omit a finalist's required checks or decide that a finalist
is ready to implement.

**What would support the intervention.** Reviewer preparation time, unresolved
queue length, or waiting time falls while the same thermal and IR-drop checks
continue to decide which packages clear review.
:::

Naming the condition that limits work is a measurement claim rather than an
impression. The observation record above supports a review constraint because
it states the work item and window, compares arrivals with completions, separates
waiting from tool runtime, and records why work repeats. Another project may
need different observations, and no single throughput limit applies to every
project.

The public AlphaChip debate shows why placement speed alone cannot diagnose a
project constraint. The 2021 AlphaChip paper reported that a reinforcement-learning method could produce
macro placements in hours [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], and a later public
disagreement turned on differences in cases, compute budgets, implementations,
and downstream physical-design checks [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. None of those comparisons measured
candidate-arrival rates, review queues, or why candidates were rejected. We use
the case here only to ask whether faster candidate production reveals what is
slowing architecture work, not to judge learned placement. Faster placement
demonstrates candidate-production speed. It does not establish that reviewer
capacity is the bottleneck or identify which part of the project limits progress.

The technical disagreement remains open, and the full evidence dispute belongs to @sec-feedback-verification-trust. The diagnostic point is that a fair
comparison must align cases, implementations, proposal and simulator budgets,
downstream checks, and the evidence required for the architectural claim. A
bottleneck claim additionally needs measurements of candidate arrival,
evaluation, review, and rejection. Matching the task, proposal count, and tool
budget can make the comparison more informative, although model inference,
human setup, prior knowledge, and total engineering work may still differ.

No single method diagnoses its own need, removes the work, and supplies the
independent check at the same time. The architect still holds the question and
its scope, the artifacts and tool outputs, the claim tied to those results, and
responsibility for the decision. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization
compares the available methods only after this work and its constraint have
been named.

\FloatBarrier

## Open Research Questions

Several questions remain open because project records support a local diagnosis
without providing universal thresholds or guarantees.

**How can a project detect that faster candidate generation has begun to delay
the decision by filling evaluation and review queues?** Arrival, completion,
waiting, and rejection behavior provide a starting point, but useful thresholds
will differ across projects.

**Which observations distinguish missing information, invalid choices,
expensive evaluation, overloaded review, and unclear decisions well enough to
choose what to fix first?** The five conditions often coexist, so a practical
diagnostic must handle more than one constraint without turning every delay
into the same category.

**How can a learned physical estimator report that a proposed topology falls
outside its tested range instead of returning a confident estimate?** Dynamic
IR drop and routing congestion are especially important cases because the
stronger physical check is expensive and may reverse an early ranking.

**What makes verification effort predictable early enough to compare it with
power, performance, area, and schedule?** A novel candidate creates coverage
and review work that is often discovered only after the architecture is
substantially fixed.

**Which change in a workload trace, compiler version, or model family
invalidates an architecture comparison?** Detecting a version change is
mechanical, but deciding whether it overturns the supported claim is not.

**How should a hardware candidate be evaluated for robustness to software drift
between design commitment and deployment?** The answer must distinguish useful
adaptability from extra hardware cost paid for changes that may never occur.

**At what design-space scale does automated search produce a better decision
than an expert-guided parameter sweep under the same evaluation and review
capacity?** The comparison must hold the problem, tool path, stopping rule,
decision criteria, and total engineering effort constant rather than compare
candidate counts alone.

**What cost model should stop a search when another round is unlikely to repay
the evaluation and review work it consumes?** Such a model must include tool
runtime, licenses, engineering attention, review, and rework rather than
inference cost alone.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Find the work limiting the decision"}
More candidates do not help when simulation capacity, expert review, stale
inputs, or an unclear decision is holding up the comparison. Before choosing
an intervention, name the work item and observation window, record where the
work waits or repeats, and state which check must remain useful.
:::


System complexity changes what a fair architecture comparison must carry.
Microarchitecture, specialization, system composition, evolving software,
physical constraints, evaluation cost, and verification add coupled work rather
than independent concerns. A project can produce candidates quickly and still
fail to reach a decision because the work needed to evaluate and review them
does not keep pace.

The chapter identified five candidate diagnoses. Information can be missing or
stale, the available choices can be unhelpful or invalid, decisive evaluation
can be too expensive, review can be overloaded, or completed analysis can lack
a clear decision. Industry trends motivate these concerns, but only project
observations can establish which one is delaying a particular comparison.

The practical move is to choose one kind of work and one observation window,
then record arrivals, completions, waiting, rework, input versions, review
outcomes, and decision closure. Existing project records can support that first
pass. Missing data leave the diagnosis unresolved. They do not justify guessing
which problem the project has.

AI is one possible intervention after the diagnosis, alongside changes to
process, capacity, or responsibility. A useful intervention changes the named
work and preserves the measurement, tool verdict, or expert review needed for
the architectural claim. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization takes
up the separate question of when
generation, prediction, optimization, or a conventional method is the right
choice.

A hardware result also inherits the software path and workload snapshot used to
produce it. Those inputs must be versioned, and a meaningful change may require
the comparison to be repeated. The result of this chapter is therefore a diagnosed
but not yet structured piece of architecture work, together with the check that
must remain useful. @sec-architecture-20-ontology shows how to formulate that
work so another architect, tool, or AI system can act on the same problem.
